title: Ryan Lucht, Datadog: From Evals to Experiments

segments.text: Okay, ladies and gentlemen, next to the
stage is Ryan Luck from Data Dog.
>> All right. I love I love lunch talks.
I've got all of what 10 minutes to
share. I'll share one idea with you in
that 10-minute span. And let's frame the
conversation here with two questions.
And the first one is one that I'm sure
you are already asking regularly or
being asked regularly, which is how do
we actually know if our AI initiatives
are working out? And the second question
maybe slightly less frequently
appreciated is how quickly do we know if
our AI initiatives are actually working
out? We could take a public example
here. This is not to pick on CLA at all
after their very successful IPO last
week. I'm sure any of us in the room
could find ourselves in this situation.
But in early 2024, they were quite
convinced that they were successfully
replacing human customer success agents
in their call centers with AI. And it
took them 14 months to then turn around
and say, "Actually, this initiative
isn't panning out as well as we hoped it
would. Customer satisfaction is
suffering a little bit. We need to
rehire some of those human customer
support agents."
The problem when it takes us a long time
to realize that something isn't working
out is that it becomes very expensive to
fail, right? Maybe we're disappointing
users and there's some hit to our
reputation as a result. Maybe we're
seating ground to our competitors if
they are successfully moving more
quickly than we are. Obviously, we've
spent a bunch of money on an idea that
didn't really work out, but there's also
the insidious hidden opportunity cost of
not having used that time to work on
something better. And let's be clear,
failure is exactly where most of our AI
initiatives are going to end up. This is
not about a sensationalized headline
from an MIT study that 95% of
initiatives are are failing or what have
you. Uh, I'll quote a much more
conservative statistic. This is from
IBM's global CEO survey. This was from
May of this year. They surveyed 2,000
CEOs. The CEO said that over the last
three years, about a quarter of AI
initiatives have delivered expected ROI.
To a skeptic or a lite, maybe this
sounds like incontrovertible proof that
uh all this AI stuff is hype, the
emperor has no clothes, etc. But this is
actually roughly exactly what I would
expect to see. I would posit that this
is part and parcel with any sort of
innovation. And here's why I say that.
If you ask the teams at tech companies
who regularly measure the success of
their ideas by running AB tests, they're
going to report very similar success
rates. This is true of UIUX design. This
is true of new product feature launches
and user flows and growth experiments,
marketing creative uh search ranking
algorithms and recommendation systems.
Most ideas we try to improve any of
these fields don't work out. The
difference and the reason that this is
okay for these teams, but it's pretty
problematic for those of us building
with AI right now, is that for these
teams who are running AB tests, they
know if their ideas are going to work
out or not in a matter of weeks, if not
days, not months or quarters. And as a
result, it's very cheap for them to
fail. So, how do we bring this power of
AB testing to make failing very cheap to
our AI initiatives? And that's what
brings us to the the title of this
little mini talk, which is from eval to
experiments, right? I would imagine most
folks in here are familiar with evals.
God knows there'll be plenty of eval
talk today and tomorrow, but we also
need to run experiments, right? Evals
help us look under the hood and and
figure out how to build what we want to
build to prioritize and tune potential
solutions is what I wrote on the slide.
But then we also need experiments to
prove the business impact of what we're
building and to make important decisions
like a ship no ship decision or a go
no-go decision or should we keep
investing down this road. It's it's kind
of like using the right tool for each
part of the process, right? Ultimately,
our goal is to solve a business problem.
This is true of any initiative AI or
otherwise. You could think of this as a
template. We want to build for use case
X in order to drive Y business outcome.
And I will give you a hint. Getting
better output from an AI model is not a
business outcome. Not even for OpenAI,
right? So let's take our our customer
support agent example here. We can say
we want to build AI powered customer
support to drive decreased support
costs. And this becomes the hypothesis
for an experiment that we're going to
run to close the feedback loop on our AI
initiative. But before we get to this
ultimate test, we have a lot of smaller
questions to answer about the how. And
that's what eval, right? They're going
to help us figure out how to approach
the build. What models do the best job
here? Do we use an open source model or
do we need to invest in a more expensive
proprietary one? Very related question.
Can we solve this affordably or cost
effectively with current technology?
here. Is it still a little bit out of
reach? What should our prompts look
like? What what sort of data set should
we feed in? Maybe how do we want to
fine-tune parameters like temperature?
So, let's talk a little bit about each
of these, right? Evals I think of as
pre-production experiments in quotation
marks. And I I use the quotation marks
because we're not doing gold standard
science here, right? The FDA does not
approve drugs on the basis of a couple
of eval. We're kind of more like
tinkering, right? So, we're going to try
out a couple different combinations of
models and parameters. We're probably
going to use a set of fixed inputs so we
can make clear comparisons between all
the things we're tweaking, right? Maybe
we have some expected inputs. Maybe we
have some atypical inputs. Maybe we even
have some adversarial inputs. We're
going to do some error analysis and look
at where our AI products are failing or
falling down today and define metrics
and evaluators based on that so that we
know what better looks like. We know
where we're steering. And then we're
going to look at those evaluators plus
maybe some prefab metrics like cost or
token usage or uh duration, latency,
tool use, what have you. So we have a
whole suite of tools inside data dog to
help with this AI observability. Uh, for
example, when you want to do that
failure mode analysis to define
evaluators and and know what we're
actually trying to improve, very helpful
to have traces of all of your actual
model calls so you can see what's going
on, code them, define evaluators. We
also have tools that help run all of
these evals and and collate and compare
the results so you can search through uh
fairly wide parameter space if you care
to and find out exactly what the the
most likely working potential solution
is.
But these pre-production eval
aren't sufficient. There's a couple
reasons for that. First, we're dealing
with limited sample sizes, right? We're
talking about running an eval maybe a
few dozen, maybe a few hundred times,
but we're almost certainly not going to
catch all of the crazy cases that are
going to happen when we set our AI
products out into the real world.
Second problem is that we're usually
dealing with text output here and
evaluating that is subjective
qualitative work and this is why uh eval
experts like KL Hussein will tell you
when you're doing that error analysis to
define evaluators have a single person
in your company or a single person at
least for the product who's doing this
and it's sort of the benevolent dictator
so that you don't run into these
subjectivity problems. Obviously that
also puts a ceiling on scale here. But
the last and the most important one is
that what looks good pre-production
often fails to correlate to the business
metrics that actually matter. This has
been true for a long time. You know, ask
any ML team that works on search
algorithms and they'll tell you that
what looks very promising in terms of a
model improvement in an offline
experiment pre-production
doesn't correlate to the metrics that
they're actually measured on when they
go out and test these things in the real
world. And that's why we need
experiments to bring our AI initiatives
to the real world. We're going to test
our solutions in real world environments
with real users. We're going to do that
gold standard science, a randomized
controlled trial to prove what works.
We're going to look at causation and not
just correlation. We're going to tie the
AI product to the business metrics like
revenue or cost and not just descriptors
of the output. And we're going to run
these experiments at scale so that we
can get insights in weeks instead of
months or quarters.
So here's what that might look like for
our customer support agent example,
right? We're going to take all of the
users that are opening support chats
with us and we're going to randomly
assign them to one of two groups. In the
A group, we have our our control group,
our placebo if you will. They're going
to continue interacting with a human
support agent just like they always
have. But half of our users are randomly
going to be selected to interface with
the AI agent. And we're going to track
thousands and thousands of people all
the way through their journey with us
after they've encountered one of these
two options. And we're going to measure
the metrics that we really care about as
a business, like did one type of
customer request returns or refunds more
often than the other? Did they make
repeat purchases with us at the same
rate? What did customer lifetime value
look like? How long did it take us to
resolve tickets? What was customer
satisfaction like? maybe what's the
all-in cost of support with human agents
versus support with AI and what the
outcome looks like is tightly quantified
causal impact of our AI products on
these business metrics. So this
screenshot is from our experimentation
platform. It's called EPO by Data Dog.
But you can see here we ran this AB test
and we proved that the AI support agent
had a positive impact on our repeat
orders and on our customer satisfaction.
This is a very clear go no-go decision.
So that's the entirety of the idea that
I want to leave you with today, right?
Is that we need to combine evals and
experiments. And when we use both tools
at the right part of our development
life cycle, we won't fall prey to long
feedback loops. We'll look at the
success metrics that actually matter,
actually keep us employed, right? And we
run ABA tests to help us go from that
idea to the proof. If you want to talk
about AI observability or
experimentation, please do drop by the
data dog booth. Thank you very much.
